doc.title: Don Menza and Sam Noto interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, January 28, 1997

title: Mancini's fortune teller and 'Another beach house'
summary: Mancini's fortune-teller story, the break with Blake Edwards, and an elevator anecdote.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: He and Pete Rugolo are great friends who wrote for, one of the arrangers who wrote for Stan Kenton in the early years, Pete Rugolo, David Rose and there’s somebody else and Mancini. They were all in Hawaii with their wives, like vacationing, in the early years. And Hank went into a fortune teller, I mean just off the street, the four of them. Everybody else went first and then Hank. And she says, “I see a great deal of success in your life,” she says, “and in your former life your name was Green.”
Which is Verdi, you know, which is Italian for Green. So we call him Joe Green.

Two weeks later, Hank was, and Hank told me this story, two weeks later he was in Los Angeles at Universal City and he was a ghost writer, and he was getting like B movies like “The Creature from the Black Lagoon” and all of that. And Blake Edwards was walking by him and he says, “Hank” he says, “I got a new series starting,” he said, “I’m going to call you next week.” He called him next week — “Mr. Lucky.” And the rest is history.
He said, “I don’t believe in any of that stuff.”
Well Monk, how are you putting up with us this long, man?
I’m just soaking it in. I love the stories.

And Hank, we’d get on an elevator and Hank was beautiful, we’d get on an elevator and you’d hear [sings “Moon River”] and you know and I’d try not to say anything, and there’s a bunch of people around us and we’re all standing there and nobody knows who Mancini is, and you know we’re all standing there and I sort of like chuckle, and I look at him, and he’d look over at me out the top of his glasses and he’d say, “Another beach house.” He was precious man.
